title: Blobby's Woodland Wonder
desc: A puzzle game where you match animals, sort stacks, and build a forest village. It's free on iOS and Android.
alt: Actual Blobby's Woodland Wonder gameplay showing animal puzzles and a floating forest
synopsis: Blobby's Woodland Wonder is a puzzle game published by ListPull, the company I founded. Players can match animals, sort stacks, build little houses, and move through a colorful woodland world. I like this project because it brings together two sides of my work that don't always show up in the same place: writing software and making something people enjoy spending time with. A game has to feel simple when you're playing it, even when there's a lot happening behind the screen. The menus, game rules, artwork, and way each level feels all have to work together. As ListPull's founder, I help guide the product and its engineering. I'm not claiming I personally created every character or visual. What I'm proud of is helping bring the whole experience together and making it available on phones.

title: Creative Studio
desc: Edit photos, add text and shapes, work with layers, and export your designs. It all runs in your browser.
alt: Illustration of the Creative Studio editor with layers, artwork, and editing controls
synopsis: Creative Studio is a browser-based editor for working with pictures and simple designs. You can bring in an image, add text or shapes, arrange things in layers, and export the result. I wanted this tool in my portfolio because it shows the kind of software I enjoy building: something practical that people can open and use without learning a complicated setup first. Editing tools are full of small decisions. A button needs to be where you expect it, the canvas needs to respond as you work, and you need to understand what you're changing. The challenge is making those details feel straightforward without losing useful options. This is part of the ListPull Studio collection, and the link takes you to the working editor. The picture here is an illustration of the tool, not a screenshot of someone's project.

title: Video Studio
desc: Cut clips, add titles, adjust audio, and export videos. You can start with a sample project.
alt: Illustration of the Video Studio timeline and video preview
synopsis: Video Studio gives people a place to put together clips in their browser. The idea is familiar: bring in video, work on a timeline, make cuts, add titles, adjust sound, and export what you've made. There's also a sample project, so someone can explore the editor before bringing their own footage. I like working on products like this because a video editor has to handle a lot without making the screen feel crowded. People need to see where they are in a clip, understand which part they're changing, and feel comfortable trying things out. Small improvements to playback controls, labels, and editing steps can make a big difference. This project also fits ListPull's wider interest in media and storytelling. The card links to the actual editor; the artwork is a visual example of its workspace.

title: AI Workspace and Code Editor
desc: Edit HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, then run the app right in your browser. An optional AI assistant can help on supported devices.
alt: Illustration of a code editor, live app preview, and optional AI chat panel
synopsis: This ListPull workspace brings coding and AI help into the same place. You can edit HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, run what you've written, and see a preview without switching between several apps. On supported devices, there's also an optional AI assistant. What interests me here is how people move from an idea to something they can test. You write a small change, run it, see what happened, and try again. That loop should feel quick and clear, especially when you're learning or experimenting. AI can help with parts of the process, but you still need to be able to read the code and judge whether the result works. I want the tool to be useful even without the assistant. This card shows an illustration, and the link opens the real workspace.

title: Business Insights
desc: Pick a sample about sales, deliveries, or wildlife, or upload a CSV. Explore the numbers with charts and comparisons.
alt: Illustration of the Business Insights data explorer with charts and sample data
synopsis: Business Insights is a way to explore a set of numbers without having to build a dashboard from scratch. You can choose a sample about inventory, customers, deliveries, or wildlife, or bring your own CSV file. From there, you can look at charts, compare values, and get a clearer picture of what's going on in the data. I like this kind of project because a useful chart is more than a line or a bar. People need to know what they're looking at, which numbers matter, and where the data came from. I spend a lot of time thinking about those details when I build data tools. The goal isn't to make every screen look busy or impressive. It's to help someone spot something they might have missed in a spreadsheet. You can open the live tool from this card.

title: Forecast Lab
desc: Use sample numbers or your own CSV to see a trend, test a forecast, and check how the model did against past data.
alt: Illustration of Forecast Lab with a line chart showing past data and a projected trend
credit: Illustration of the live tool, example values
synopsis: Forecast Lab lets you take a set of past numbers and see what a model thinks might happen next. You can start with sample data or upload a CSV, look at the trend, run a forecast, and compare the model with earlier results. I've also worked on forecasting services using Node.js and ARIMA, so this is an area I know from the engineering side as well. The most important part for me is keeping the difference between real data and an estimate easy to see. A forecast can be useful without being certain, and the screen shouldn't pretend otherwise. Charts need clear labels, sensible time ranges, and room for a result that isn't perfect. This is a tool for exploring patterns, not a promise about the future. The illustration uses example values, and the link opens the app.

title: ListPull Wildlife Media
desc: Nature videos, wildlife stories, and game updates shared through ListPull's channels.
alt: Illustrated wildlife media gallery with a bird, trees, and nature video cards
synopsis: ListPull has always been interested in nature, animals, and the kinds of stories people want to share. Alongside our games and software tools, the company publishes wildlife videos, short clips, and updates across its channels. I wanted to keep that side of the company in my portfolio because it explains why our work doesn't fit into just one box. Sometimes we're building an app. Sometimes we're thinking about how a story looks, sounds, or reaches people. Those things influence each other. Working around media has made me pay closer attention to how images, timing, and simple navigation change the way someone experiences a product. The linked videos and posts are company-published work. I'm not claiming to have filmed or edited every piece of wildlife footage myself. The image on this card is an original illustration, not a video still.

title: Clinic Recommendations
desc: I led work on a React feature that helped find relevant clinics using lab data. Behind it were AWS services, PostgreSQL, Bedrock, and OpenSearch.
alt: Simplified diagram of the clinical recommendation pipeline, not a client screen
synopsis: At Accenture, I led engineering work on a clinic recommendation feature for Bristol Myers Squibb. The feature was added to an existing React application and used lab information to help surface relevant clinic options. On the back end, the work involved AWS Step Functions, Lambda, PostgreSQL, Bedrock embeddings, and OpenSearch. My role included helping the team connect these pieces and make the result usable in the application people already had. What I took away from this project is that AI features don't live on their own. They still need dependable data, clear rules, careful testing, and an interface that makes sense to the person using it. This was also sensitive work, so the portfolio doesn't show private data or a real client screen. The diagram is a simplified view of how the systems fit together, not a copy of the production setup.

title: Public Health Systems
desc: I helped connect Salesforce and AWS Connect for public health call centers. I also worked on digital vaccination records and disease tracking tools.
role: Application architect and senior engineer · Accenture
alt: Simplified diagram of public health system integrations, not a client screen
synopsis: At Accenture, I worked on public health systems that had to pass information between different tools and teams. One part of the work connected Salesforce contact center operations with AWS Connect, so calls and follow-up steps could move through a more organized process. I also worked on digital vaccination record access and disease tracking workflows. These projects taught me how much time can be lost when people have to repeat a step or copy information from one system to another. The technical work included APIs, cloud services, routing rules, and data handling, but the reason for building them was practical: make the work easier for the people doing it. I worked as a senior engineer and later in an architecture leadership role. The image is a general diagram, not a government system or an actual patient record.

title: Bureau of Labor Statistics Website
desc: I helped modernize the BLS website with React components, clearer data charts, and tools that made publishing easier.
alt: Illustration of a public data dashboard, not an official BLS screenshot
synopsis: At BAE Systems, I helped modernize the public Bureau of Labor Statistics website for the U.S. Department of Labor. I worked on reusable React components, charts built with Highcharts, and pages that pulled in government data through APIs. I also wrote tests and helped with publishing tools for articles, images, and PDFs. This kind of work isn't flashy, but it matters. People visit public data websites because they need to find a number, understand a chart, or check something they heard. If the page is hard to use or the data is presented poorly, the information isn't doing its job. I learned a lot about accessibility, careful testing, and keeping a large website consistent while different teams work on it. The image here is an illustration, not an official BLS screenshot. You can follow the link to the public site.
